issues.subcategory: Tension in the cultural-niche framing of improvements
issues.description: Tension in the cultural-niche framing of improvements: In the opening theoretical framing, the phrase “well-understood improvements” is in tension with the next sentence’s claim that optimization can arise “in the absence of explicit understanding.” Since the paper’s contrast between causal-reasoning and cultural-transmission accounts turns on whether improvements require causal understanding, this wording makes the cultural-niche mechanism harder to parse.
issues.quote: The cultural niche hypothesis suggests that complex technologies like bows result from the accumulation of many, mostly small, well-understood improvements made across generations linked by cultural transmission 1,9,14. Over time, the selective retention of improvements gives rise to highly optimized solutions in the absence of explicit understanding about how these solutions work.

issues.subcategory: Figure 1 caption blurs CoM height and acceleration
issues.description: Figure 1 caption blurs CoM height and acceleration: The CoM explanation in the Figure 1 caption appears to compress two distinct effects. An off-axis CoM improves initial acceleration only when its horizontal/rotational offset supplies torque in the downhill direction; a higher initial CoM points instead to gravitational potential energy available over subsequent motion. Because the caption moves from “better initial acceleration” to “higher initial position,” panels C-D could be read as treating height alone as the acceleration mechanism, although the Methods section later distinguishes these effects.
issues.quote: Figure 1 | Experimental task and design. A) Illustration of the physical system used in the experiment. The wheel had 4 radial spokes, and one weight could be moved along each spoke. The time it takes for the wheel to cover the track was determined by its moment of inertia and the position of its centre of mass. A-B) The moment of inertia depends on how mass is distributed around the axis. Wheel A has a smaller moment of inertia and spins faster than wheel B. C-D) Asymmetrical wheels do not have their centre of mass on the axis of rotation, which can give wheels better initial acceleration. Wheel $C$ covers the distance faster than wheel $D$ due to the higher initial position of its centre of mass.

issues.subcategory: Interval terminology in the first Results paragraph
issues.description: Interval terminology in the first Results paragraph: The interval terminology is inconsistent in this paragraph: the Generation effects are labelled as $95\%$ Confidence Intervals / CI, while the Methods state that the models are Bayesian and use $95\%$ credible intervals, and the next sentence reports HPDIs. This leaves the intended posterior interval summary for these Generation effects unclear.
issues.quote: Results confirm these predictions. The average wheel speed (calculated as $1 \mathrm{~m} /$ descent time) increased across generations (Generation $95 \%$ Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02), mean $=5.37 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{h}$, Figure 2.A) while participants' understanding did not (Generation $95 \% \mathrm{CI}$ : ( $-0.54,0.25$ ), mean $=-0.04$, Figure 2.B). The average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was $123.6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{h}$ ( $95 \%$ Highest Posterior Density Interval: (117.3, 130.6)) and their understanding score was 4.60

issues.subcategory: Unclear 71% optimization calculation in Results
issues.description: Unclear 71% optimization calculation in Results: The $71\%$ optimization figure appears to come from closing the gap between the first-generation estimate and the physical maximum using four times the generation slope, $4 \times 5.37/(154-123.6) \approx 71\%$. Because this calculation is not stated and using the displayed fifth-generation mean gives a slightly different percentage, the baseline and normalization for this percentage are not fully transparent.
issues.quote: After 5 generations, average wheel speed increased to $145.7 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{h}(95 \% \mathrm{HPDI}:(138.5,152.4)$ ) while participants' understanding remained the same ( $95 \% \mathrm{HPDI}:(3.65,5.39)$, mean $=4.47$ ). Given that the maximum possible speed was about $154 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{h}$, these results indicate an optimization of $71 \%$ after only four cultural generations. This confirms that the retention of improvements over generations produces highly optimized solutions and need not depend on the emergence of more accurate causal models.

issues.subcategory: Aggregate understanding claim in theory-treatment results
issues.description: Aggregate understanding claim in theory-treatment results: The conclusion about individual understanding is broader than the aggregate model can support. Analysis 4 is reported on total understanding score after removing the Physical Principle terms, whereas the subsequent Figure 3 analysis argues that theory content shifts principle-specific understanding. This passage would be more accurate if the null/weak result were limited to aggregate or overall understanding rather than understanding in general.
issues.quote:
Results show that the average wheel speed increased at a similar rate in the "Configurations + Theory" as it did in the "Configurations" treatment (Treatment $95 \% \mathrm{Cl}:(-10.76,18.13)$, mean $=3.52 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{h}$; Generation $\times$ Treatment $95 \% \mathrm{Cl}$ : (-7.07, 2.52), mean $=-2.23 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{h}$, Figure 2.A) and that participants' understanding again barely changed across generations, although participants in the very last generation had a slightly better understanding when they had inherited a theory (Treatment $95 \% \mathrm{Cl}:(-2.54,0.31)$, mean $=-1.14$; Generation $\times$ Treatment $95 \% \mathrm{Cl}:(0.03,0.81)$, mean $=0.44$, Figure 2.B). Thus, these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal
theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding.

issues.subcategory: Dismissal of credible interaction effect
issues.description: Dismissal of credible interaction effect: The concluding sentence is too broad relative to the reported aggregate-understanding interaction. The Generation $\times$ Treatment interval for understanding, $(0.03, 0.81)$, excludes zero and is described just beforehand as a slight last-generation advantage for participants who inherited a theory. The text can still characterize the effect as small and note the absence of a speed effect, but it should not present the analyses as simply lacking support for any effect on individual understanding.
issues.quote:
although participants in the very last generation had a slightly better understanding when they had inherited a theory (Treatment $95 \% \mathrm{Cl}:(-2.54,0.31)$, mean $=-1.14$; Generation $\times$ Treatment $95 \% \mathrm{Cl}:(0.03,0.81)$, mean $=0.44$, Figure 2.B). Thus, these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal
theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding.

issues.subcategory: Physics error regarding initial acceleration
issues.description: Physics error regarding initial acceleration: The parenthetical about 'better initial acceleration' is imprecise. In the Methods, the initial-acceleration advantage of the top-and-right strategy is attributed to the right weight's greater leverage, while the top weight initially applies a vertical force on the axis and does not add initial angular momentum. As written, the Results sentence could be read as attributing better initial acceleration to both extreme top and right weights rather than to the right-weight/centre-of-mass offset.
issues.quote: In contrast, participants who inherited a centre-of-mass theory produced unbalanced wheels with their top and right weights at extreme positions (i.e. with better initial acceleration, Figure 3C and G).

issues.subcategory: Confounded comparison of exploration variance
issues.description: Confounded comparison of exploration variance: The Figure 3 comparison does not by itself isolate the effect of inherited theory content from the configurations transmitted with it. Because these theory-type comparisons are exploratory, the causal language about inherited theories constraining exploration and preventing participants from noticing other variables is too strong. Participants in the theory subgroups inherited both a written theory and the predecessor’s last two wheel configurations, and theory type is likely correlated with those inherited configurations and chain histories. Thus, narrower exploration patterns and the associated understanding scores could partly reflect anchoring or local search around transmitted wheels rather than the written theory alone. It is difficult to attribute the later understanding sub-score differences specifically to receiving an inertia-related versus centre-of-mass-related written theory; the causal language about specific theories reducing or increasing understanding should be qualified or supported by a configuration-conditioned comparison. Ultimately, the evidence supports a plausible canalization mechanism rather than a fully isolated causal effect of the written theory itself.
issues.quote: Participants who did not inherit any theory ( $N=70$ ) sampled various positions along each spoke ( $A$ ) and their wheels' centres of mass were concentrated in the upper-right quadrant (E). Participants who inherited an inertia theory ( $\mathrm{N}=15$ ) mainly produced compact and balanced wheels (B-F). Participants who inherited a centre-of-mass theory ( $\mathrm{N}=17$ ) produced unbalanced wheels with their top and right weights at extreme positions (C-G). The few participants who inherited a full theory (N=6) produced compact and asymmetrical wheels (D-H). Inheriting an inertia theory reduces understanding about centre of mass and increases understanding about inertia

issues.subcategory: Causal mediation claim around Figure 3I
issues.description: Causal mediation claim around Figure 3I: The Supplementary Figure 2 analysis is consistent with the proposed exploration pathway, but it does not really identify the mediation mechanism. The groups are defined by participants' self-selected exploration behavior, and without baseline understanding measures it is difficult to rule out the possibility that prior intuitions or partial understanding drove both the chosen wheels and the later sub-score pattern.
issues.quote: One explanation for this pattern is that inheriting a unidimensional theory makes individuals focus on the effect of one parameter while blinding them to the effects of others. However, participants' understanding may also result from different exploration patterns. For instance, participants who received an inertia-related theory mainly produced balanced wheels (Figure 3F), which could have prevented them from observing the effect of varying the position of the wheel's centre of mass. To test this mechanism, we grouped participants who did not inherit any theory (i.e. from the "Configurations" treatment) into 3 categories: those who produced various types of wheels, those who only produced balanced wheels, and those who only produced unbalanced wheels. Participants who produced various types of wheels scored similarly on questions about inertia and centre of mass. However, participants who only produced balanced wheels showed better understanding of inertia than centre of mass, and participants who only produced unbalanced wheels showed better understanding of centre of mass than inertia (Supplementary Figure 2). These results suggest that the understanding patterns observed in participants who received unidimensional theories is likely the result of the canalizing effect of theory transmission on exploration.

issues.subcategory: Performance-neutral claim is unclear here
issues.description: Performance-neutral claim is unclear here: The claim that the canalizing effect is 'performance-neutral' is ambiguous here. The explanation refers to compensation between inertia and centre-of-mass understanding sub-scores, whereas 'performance' elsewhere mainly refers to wheel speed; the passage does not clearly establish why offsetting understanding scores would imply neutral consequences for wheel performance. While the paper shows no clear aggregate benefit of theory transmission for wheel speed, compensation between inertia and centre-of-mass understanding sub-scores does not by itself show that canalized exploration has neutral performance consequences in the artifact-design task.
issues.quote: These results suggest that the understanding patterns observed in participants who received unidimensional theories is likely the result of the canalizing effect of theory transmission on exploration. Note that in the present case, this canalizing effect is performance-neutral: with our 2-dimensional problem, better understanding of one dimension and worse understanding of one dimension simply compensate each other. For a many-dimensional problem, though, better understanding of one dimension is unlikely to compensate for worse understanding of all the others.

issues.subcategory: Overclaim about mixed-gender settings in discussion
issues.description: Overclaim about mixed-gender settings in discussion: The discussion overstates external validity here: the experiment used sex-segregated, sequential chains of isolated individual participants, so the paper does not directly support the claim that the findings generalize to mixed-gender collaborative settings.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings. Instead they mainly produce unidimensional models related to a specifically salient dimension 18. Although evidence of individual' erroneous theories of motion are sometimes considered as experimental artefacts resulting from impoverished stimuli

issues.subcategory: Acceleration inference in final discussion is unclear
issues.description: Acceleration inference in final discussion is unclear: The inference from centre-of-mass locations to appropriate intuitions about maximizing acceleration is too compressed. A centre of mass in the upper-right quadrant fits the paper’s dynamics account, but a centered centre of mass only supports that interpretation if paired with additional information about inertia or weight placement.
issues.quote: It is worth noting that despite exhibiting poor understanding of the experimental physical system, participants did not randomly explore the parameter space. For example, in both treatments, wheels were much more likely to have their centre of mass at the center of the wheel, or in the upper right quadrant. This indicates that participants had appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration, and sampled the parameter space fairly efficiently in that regard. Our ability to restrict exploration to potentially useful portions of the design space certainly accelerated cultural evolution in our experiment.

issues.subcategory: Biased exploration is overread as intuition
issues.description: Biased exploration is overread as intuition: The inference from aggregate non-random sampling to participants having appropriate intuitions should be treated cautiously. The observed patterns are consistent with useful exploration biases, but they do not by themselves distinguish prior intuition from within-task feedback, inherited configurations, or selection across chains.
issues.quote: It is worth noting that despite exhibiting poor understanding of the experimental physical system, participants did not randomly explore the parameter space. For example, in both treatments, wheels were much more likely to have their centre of mass at the center of the wheel, or in the upper right quadrant. This indicates that participants had appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration, and sampled the parameter space fairly efficiently in that regard. Our ability to restrict exploration to potentially useful portions of the design space certainly accelerated cultural evolution in our experiment.

issues.subcategory: Garbled mechanics in "Dynamics of the wheel"
issues.description: Garbled mechanics in "Dynamics of the wheel": The mechanics summary in this paragraph is technically imprecise in two places. A smaller moment of inertia reduces the torque needed for a given angular acceleration or target angular speed, but not for a specified increase in angular momentum over a specified time. The centre-of-mass sentence also compresses energy conversion, torque, and angular-momentum change in a way that leaves the relevant axis or comparison unclear, even though later text partly clarifies the intended tradeoff. Specifically, the advantage of this upper-right configuration depends on the gravitational torque produced by the off-axis centre of mass at the initial orientation and on the rolling direction; as written, the sentence may suggest a direct energy-to-angular-momentum mechanism without specifying those conditions.
issues.quote: The performance of the wheel depends on two variables: its moment of inertia and the position of its centre of mass. The wheel's moment of inertia depends on how mass is distributed around its axis of rotation. Wheels with a smaller moment of inertia (i.e. wheels that have their weights closer to the axis) require less torque to increase angular momentum and spin faster (Movies are available at osf.io/afwmr). Asymmetrical wheels do not have their centre of mass on the axis of rotation, which can give wheels better initial acceleration. When the centre of mass of the wheel is in the wheel's upper right quadrant, more energy is converted into angular kinetic energy so that the wheel will benefit from higher increases in angular momentum.

issues.subcategory: Incorrect physical description of adding mass to the axis
issues.description: Incorrect physical description of adding mass to the axis: The statement that adding two 500-gram plates along the axis reduces the wheel’s moment of inertia is physically inaccurate if moment of inertia means the absolute rotational inertia of the wheel. Adding mass at or near the axis cannot reduce absolute moment of inertia; the intended point may instead be that the added central mass reduces centre-of-mass displacement or changes the effective inertia-to-mass ratio.
issues.quote: Two 500 -gram weight plates were positioned along the axis of the wheel (one on each side of the clamp) in order to reduce the wheel's moment of inertia and limit the occurrence of motionless or back-spinning configurations.

issues.subcategory: Understanding score needs an explicit scoring rule
issues.description: Understanding score needs an explicit scoring rule: The understanding outcome is not explicitly scored in the Methods. The text describes 10 three-option test responses, but the later models use Score without stating the item-level rule, including how No difference responses were treated and whether Score is the number correct out of 10 or a transformed measure.
issues.quote: After completing the task, participants were told that they would be presented with pairs of wheels and that they must guess which one of 2 wheels would descend the rails faster. They were also told that one of their answers will be randomly selected at the end of the test and that 5 euros will be added to their gain if that answer is correct. For each pair, participants could submit 3 possible answers: "Wheel 1", "Wheel 2" or "No difference". Participants could take as much time as needed before submitting their answer. Once an answer was submitted, another pair of wheels was displayed until participants compared 10 pairs of wheels.

issues.subcategory: Payoff formula unclear for failures in Participants’ payoff
issues.description: Payoff formula unclear for failures in Participants’ payoff: The payoff rule is under-specified for non-descending wheels and for any recorded speeds below MinSpeed. Because the formula’s linear term is $3(\text{RecordedSpeed}-96)/64$, it would be negative unless failures or very slow wheels were clipped, assigned a minimum speed, or otherwise handled; the text only says that the bonus is 0 for non-descending wheels.
issues.quote:
The following equation determined the payoff of each wheel:

$$
[1 \text { - }((\text { MaxSpeed - RecordedSpeed }) /(\text { MaxSpeed - MinSpeed }))] \times 3+\text { Bonus }
$$

with MaxSpeed $=160$, MinSpeed $=96$. RecordedSpeed was the recorded average speed of the wheel. Bonus took the value 0.2 for wheels that descended and 0 otherwise.

Participants' final payoff corresponded to the sum of the payoff of each of their wheels plus the payoff of the next participant' first two wheels plus $5 €$ if they correctly answered the randomly selected test.

issues.subcategory: Rater agreement statistic unclear in Theory coding
issues.description: Rater agreement statistic unclear in Theory coding: The reliability statistic for theory coding is not fully interpretable as written. Three coders are described, but the paper reports Cohen’s kappa without specifying whether the values are pairwise kappas, averaged pairwise kappas, comparisons to a consensus code, or a multi-rater agreement statistic.
issues.quote: 3 individuals blind to the research question were explained the dynamics of the wheel (i.e. the respective role of inertia and centre of mass in the performance of the wheel) and were asked to code participants' theories according to whether they contain accurate information related to moment of inertia and/or centre of mass. A theory contained information related to moment of inertia when it says that the wheels goes faster when its weights are close to the axis (e.g. "The wheel covers the track faster when its weights are balanced and close to the axis.").

issues.subcategory: Model selection sits uneasily with “Preregistered” label
issues.description: Model selection sits uneasily with “Preregistered” label: Analysis 1 is labeled preregistered, but the final model specification is said to have been selected by comparing candidate models fitted to the observed data. Unless the candidate set and selection criterion were themselves preregistered, this makes the confirmatory status of the reported model unclear.
issues.quote: Preregistered analysis 1 investigated the average speed of wheels across generations in the Configurations treatment. Data were restricted to participants' last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset. We fitted a linear model with "Speed" as the outcome variable, "Trial", "Generation" as predictor variables and "Player's identity" and "Chain's identity" as random effects (see Supplementary Table 1 for model output). The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.

issues.subcategory: Unsound statistical justification for aggregating scores
issues.description: Unsound statistical justification for aggregating scores: The deviation from the preregistered principle-specific understanding model is under-justified. Aggregating inertia and centre-of-mass scores after a nonconvergent model changes the estimand to total understanding and can mask principle-specific changes; the text does not explain why alternative specifications for the two-score structure were unsuitable.
issues.quote: However, analyses revealed that understanding scores about inertia and centre of mass were negatively correlated (Supplementary Figure 9 and Supplementary Table 7) and some individuals better understood inertia than centre of mass while others better understood centre of mass than inertia (Figure 3I and Supplementary Figure 2). As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable "Physical Principle" in the reported model.

{"overall": "Here are some observations on the current manuscript, focusing on how the experimental design aligns with the core theoretical claims.

**Measurement of causal understanding**

The headline claims, including the Abstract and Results, suggest that optimization occurred in the absence of explicit causal understanding. Readers may note that the understanding metric—a post-task prediction over ten fixed-order static wheel pairs—measures predictive discrimination and perhaps intuitive physics heuristics, rather than the explicit possession of causal models. Exploratory results show above-chance principle-specific performance in the Configurations treatment, as well as non-random exploration guided by appropriate intuitions. 

Aggregating the results into a 0–10 score obscures the divergence between inertia and centre-of-mass understanding, which is visible in Figure 3I and Supplementary Figure 2. The evidence might more securely support a claim that understanding is incomplete or multi-dimensionally fragmented, rather than entirely absent. Incorporating item- or principle-level modeling to link understanding directly to performance, or framing the finding to state that optimization outpaces the accumulation of explicit multidimensional understanding, would calibrate the analysis more closely to the data.

**Establishing the cultural accumulation baseline**

The experiment demonstrates that lineages of social learners produce faster wheels over time. However, it is difficult to determine whether intergenerational transmission achieves more than simply extending a trail-and-error search across 25 total trials. Because a Generation 5 participant leverages the products of prior search through the last two configurations and scores, the speed improvement from $123.6$ m/h to $145.7$ m/h is entirely compatible with extended individual trial-and-error. 

Without an isolated 25-trial individual learning baseline, or an analytical method separating within-participant improvement from improvements strictly retained across participants, the design does not cleanly isolate a specifically cultural mechanism from a distributed, cumulative search process. Clarifying this distinction would strengthen the argument that social transmission is the active ingredient.

**Integration of failures into speed metrics**

The main optimization models are restricted to participants' last two trials to limit the impact of non-descending wheels, while Figure 2 plots failures separately. The Methods indicate that no data points were excluded. Because the plotted speed lines average only the non-failure wheels, any changes in failure rates across generations or treatments could inflate the appearance of optimization or mask genuine treatment differences. 

Incorporating failures directly into the performance measurement—perhaps through the payoff metric, penalized speed models, or a hurdle model analyzing descent probability alongside conditional speed—would yield a more robust measure of optimization. Additionally, the $71\%$ optimization figure requires clearer derivation. The text references a maximum possible speed of $154$ m/h, while the actual payoff formula uses a MaxSpeed of $160$. Reconciling these numbers will prevent confusion regarding the terminal level of optimization achieved.

**Scope of the theory transmission conclusions**

The manuscript concludes that the transmission of causal models has no noticeable effect on cultural evolution. The intervals for treatment, Generation $\times$ Treatment, and late-generation understanding are not framed around equivalence tests against a predefined smallest meaningful effect. 

The manipulation itself involves participants writing short theories after only five trials, restricted to under 340 characters, and prompted by the structured phrase "The wheel covers the distance faster when...". This effectively tests the transmission of nascent, novice heuristics. Broad conclusions about the utility of transmitting explicit technological knowledge or historically vetted causal instruction do not strictly follow from this paradigm. The Abstract and Discussion would benefit from narrowing this conclusion to reflect the transmission of early-stage heuristics.

**Endogeneity in inherited theories**

The proposition that inaccurate inherited theories canalize exploration and shape downstream understanding is a compelling addition to the literature. A vulnerability here is that theory content was not randomly assigned. It was generated by preceding participants and therefore likely covaries with inherited configurations, chain history, and previous performance. 

Furthermore, the subgroup counts are small—particularly for full theories ($N = 6$)—which makes the heat-map comparisons in Figure 3 susceptible to over-interpretation. While the balanced/unbalanced comparison in the Configurations treatment is suggestive, it cannot isolate theory content as the definitive cause of exploration differences. Softening the causal language in the Abstract and Results, or fitting models that control for inherited configuration, generation, and received performance, will protect these findings from methodological critique.

**Extrapolating from low-dimensional design spaces**

The Introduction frames the wheel’s low-dimensional structure as a conservative test of the hypothesis relative to complex technologies like kayaks or bows. One could argue the inverse: a two-principle physical system that provides immediate feedback over repeated trials is uniquely permissive to biased trial-and-error and local hill-climbing. 

This makes the experiment a powerful demonstration of how optimization operates without explicit multidimensional understanding in bounded systems. However, it provides a weaker foundation for broad claims regarding high-dimensional, rugged design spaces.
